The future of air combat just showed up in the skies over California, and it looks like one fighter pilot flying with a robot. In a recent test out of Edwards Air Force Base, a US Air Force F-22 Raptor pilot acted as an airborne "quarterback," sending high-level orders to an AI-controlled drone wingman, Anduril's YFQ-44A "Fury," that flew alongside the jet and carried them out on its own.

The pilot didn't steer it with a joystick; he told it what he wanted, and its software worked out how. The Fury is one of a new class of cheaper, uncrewed "loyal wingman" drones the Air Force wants flying alongside its fighters, adding numbers, sensors, and options without putting more pilots at risk. The Air Force has talked about eventually fielding at least 1,000 of them.

A human still calls the plays. But the vision is clear: one day, a single pilot directing a small team of intelligent drones, with the machines doing the most dangerous flying. It's no longer a concept video. It's a test result.

Always ready to drop in where we are needed. 

Soldiers conduct fast-rope insertion/extraction system training, a crucial skill for getting boots on the ground in a hurry. 

📷 Army Sgt. Duke Edwards

For years, hypersonic weapons have been the rarest and most expensive things in the American arsenal, a handful of exquisite, hand-built systems that cost a fortune per shot. A three-year-old startup is trying to flip that completely. On October 8, a company called Castelion, founded by former SpaceX engineers, posted a photo of its new hypersonic, named Blackbeard, streaking out of a launcher mounted on the back of a mobility truck. Their slogan for the image said it all: "Built to move with the fight."

The big idea isn't that Blackbeard is faster than other hypersonics. It's that it's cheap. Castelion wants to build these at scale and at low cost, so that a hypersonic can be treated less like a national treasure and more like ordinary ammunition, something you can fire freely instead of rationing. The Army's target is to get roughly 80 percent of the capability of its planned next-generation precision missile at a fraction of the cost per round.

That's a genuine break from how the U.S. has done this. The Army's other hypersonic, the Dark Eagle, is powerful but relies on large, specialized, expensive launch equipment. Blackbeard is designed to fire from the kind of mobile launchers the Army already uses, like the fire-control system behind HIMARS, and the ground-launched version is a compact two-stage design with a maneuvering payload. Castelion has hinted at a range of just under 500 miles, though it hasn't released full performance numbers.

And the military is backing it with real money. The Navy is already working to fit Blackbeard onto the F/A-18 Super Hornet, flew a developmental test with the missiles under a jet in September, and put down a 105 million dollar contract earlier this year. The Pentagon has signaled that once testing is done, it plans a multi-year deal for at least 500 missiles a year, and it's seeking the funding to buy more than 12,000 over five years. A production-representative Army launch is planned for 2027.

None of this is proven yet, the hardest tests are still ahead, and the real-world performance of the production version is still under wraps. But the direction is what matters. For a long time, America's answer to hypersonics was a small number of incredibly expensive ones. Blackbeard is a bet that the better answer is thousands of cheap ones you can fire off the back of a truck. If it works, it doesn't just add a new weapon, it changes the math of a fight. That's why a company barely three years old suddenly has the full attention of the Pentagon.

There are few images more sacred to the United States military than the flag-raising on Iwo Jima, six men hauling the Stars and Stripes up a pole on Mount Suribachi in February 1945, frozen forever in Joe Rosenthal's photograph. A stone version of that moment stands near the National Museum of the Marine Corps, just outside the gates of Quantico. This week, a man walked up to it with a sledgehammer.

On October 21, in Triangle, Virginia, police got a call about someone vandalizing the memorial. When officers arrived, they found a 27-year-old man attacking the limestone statue and took him into custody without incident. By the time he was stopped, he had knocked the head clean off one of the figures and done enough other damage that the repair bill is expected to run into the hundreds of thousands of dollars. He has been charged with felony destruction of property and injury to a monument, and is being held without bond. Police have not offered a motive.

To understand why this stings the way it does, you have to understand what the statue means. It's a smaller version of the Marine Corps War Memorial sculpted by Felix de Weldon, the bronze original that was dedicated in Arlington on the Marine Corps' birthday in 1954. The site near Quantico isn't just a roadside landmark. It's where Marines hold promotions, commissionings, retirements, and reenlistments. For generations of Marines, some of the proudest moments of their careers happened standing in front of that flag.

And the men it depicts were real. The figure believed to have been struck is Cpl. Harlon Block, who helped raise that flag and was killed in action on Iwo Jima just days later, one of nearly 7,000 Americans who gave their lives taking that small volcanic island. The statue was never really about the stone. It's about them.

The museum's director, Keil Gentry, says the repairs will be challenging, and experts are already being consulted. The statue will be rebuilt, the head restored, the damage undone. But a memorial's power was never in the material. You can take a sledgehammer to the figure of Harlon Block. You cannot touch what he and the others did on that mountain, or the reverence the Corps still holds for it. That outlasts any act of vandalism, and it always will.

That New Bradley Smell

How's this for a new ride? Pfc. James Hays gets behind the wheel of a newly fielded M2A4E1 Bradley Fighting Vehicle. The fielding equips the brigade with upgraded Bradleys featuring improved protection, targeting and environmental-control capabilities.

📷 Army Sgt. Julian A. Winston
